articles.title: Education for society
articles.content: NOTWITHSTANDING what might be going on in other countries, Pakistan has a real problem regarding violence against women. In the past few months alone, we have seen some horrendous incidents: ‘honour’ killings, marriage-of-choice killings, rapes, domestic violence, spousal violence and killings, abduction, rape and killing of minors, and violence against employees and staff. There is no dearth of reports from national and international bodies documenting the extent and severity of these issues. A couple of points stand out in these reports. One, we do not have good data on violence against women. Incidents are underreported, and there are no national registries or data sets of any sort. Most reported data comes from newspaper reporting, police case registrations, hotline reports, and so on. Two, though many reasons — poor laws and weak implementation, few protections, pathetic institutional arrangements, low reporting and conviction rates, delays, social and societal taboos, etc — are cited in these reports, a primary one is the impact of patriarchy: the control of men over society. Patriarchy shapes not only laws, norms, and expectations in this society; it also shapes responses: what she was wearing, why she was out at that time, why she was driving, and so on. Patriarchy is hard to spot, fight, and neutralise because it is embedded in almost every norm, rule, and law. Most societies have, historically and even today, used education to address society’s main issues. What it means to be educated has varied across societies and times, and one element (other than the ability to carry out tasks) has been the larger socialisation of the individual within society and the shaping of their values and norms. I want to pose the question: should we not be shaping our education to take on the issue of patriarchy and its impacts directly? Recently, my daughter started school as a fifth-grader in a public school in London. On the very first day, after introductions and other formalities, her teacher spent a couple of hours talking about the autism spectrum and notions of inclusion, expected behaviour, and what was not expected or what would not be tolerated. This came before any conversation about the English or math curriculum. This term, the heroes the class will be introduced to include Frida Kahlo, Mahatma Gandhi, Simone Biles, and a couple of human rights defenders from across the globe. We must address the most urgent social and cultural issues of our society through education. Every day when I walk her back from school and ask her about her day, she tells me about the book they have been reading in class, the documentary they saw, the discussions they had, etc. I have to ask specifically about her math, English and history lessons. They are there, and she is learning the subjects she is supposed to, but the school and her education are much more than that. This has been true every school day. It is about what she needs as a human being and a citizen; it is about values and the kind of society that needs to be there. Specific skills are just a small part of the ‘education’ she is getting. I went to some of the best schools in Lahore in the day. But when I landed in England for undergraduate studies, one of the first things I noticed, comparing my own educational experiences with those of my undergraduate peers from England, was that almost each one of my peers had been exposed to things I had not. All of them had good exposure to and knowledge of a major European language other than English. All of them had studied music for many years in their schools, and many could play one instrument fairly well or had a good understanding of it. Many of them had had singing lessons: some were good choir singers. So, language, music and singing. Their exposure to art was also more advanced than mine. The schools I attended focused much more on doing well in academic subjects and preparing for school-leaving examinations. Though schools, especially high-fee private schools, have changed a lot, including in Pakistan over the years, even the best of them today remain narrowly focused on subject understanding and examination performance. They do not give any importance to preparing citizens and human beings. Nor is there a demand for this from parents. In fact, the trend, at least in public schools, is the opposite. With clear evidence that most children in schools are not learning enough (77 per cent are ‘learning poor’), the focus has shifted to foundational learning to ensure students grasp the basics of language and math. But the danger is that this approach narrows the scope of education even more. We focus on only essential learning objectives and try to drill them into students. We teach these and test only these. We test only these, so we teach only these. Foundational learning is the flavour right now, and it is hard even to raise concerns about what this might mean for broader educational objectives. Education has always been about creating citizens and human beings who can take us forward. We must address the most pressing social and cultural issues of our society through education. If we do not, what is the point of education, and how else can we plan for a better society? Violence against women, in all its forms, and the grip of patriarchy on our society is exactly the kind of embedded issue that cannot be tackled through law alone and has to be challenged through education and with a sense of purpose. The sheer brutality of what we keep seeing should wake us up to the urgency with which this needs to be addressed. The writer is a senior research fellow at the Institute of Development and Economic Alternatives and an associate professor of economics at Lums.
articles.author: Faisal Bari

articles.title: Safeguarding and harnessing AI
articles.content: THE launch of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation in Shanghai on July 16, 2026, may mark an important moment in global AI governance. Initiated by China, the body aims to promote cooperation and keep AI beneficial, safe and fair. It has attracted 29 countries, mostly from the Global South, and is expected to grow. To become globally effective, WAICO must broaden its membership across North and South and evolve into a genuinely multilateral institution. President Xi Jinping summarised its ambition: AI development, he said, should not be “a solo performance by a single country, but a symphony of international cooperation”. WAICO emerges amid a technological dilemma. Like nuclear technology, AI promises major benefits but also raises fears of misuse, instability and harm. The new organisation’s task is not simply to control AI, but to also manage risks while widening access to benefits without discrimination. Its founders should therefore study the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which faced a similar challenge almost seven decades ago. The atomic bomb demonstrated that nuclear technology could transform the strategic balance between nations and threaten civilisation; the same science also offered advances in medicine, agriculture, industry and energy. The challenge was to prevent destructive applications and share peaceful benefits. President Dwight Eisenhower’s ‘Atoms for Peace’ address to the UN General Assembly in 1953 proposed an international agency to make nuclear technology available for peaceful purposes “for the benefit of all mankind”. His initiative led to the IAEA’s creation in 1957. The IAEA was never merely a nuclear policeman. Its statute covered peaceful applications, scientific exchange, training, safeguards and safety standards. Its founding principle was to make nuclear technology safer without denying humanity its benefits — a central lesson for WAICO. Safeguards became a core IAEA function, assuring states that civilian nuclear materials and activities were not diverted to military purposes. After the 1968 Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, they became central to the global non-proliferation regime. Yet the Agency also helped countries acquire knowledge, train personnel, build infrastructure and use nuclear science peacefully. An organisation that only prohibits will meet resistance; one that also advances legitimate development creates stronger cooperation. The IAEA’s institutional logic offers five useful lessons for the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation. The IAEA developed complementary roles in verification, peaceful uses, technical cooperation, safety and security. As nuclear technology spread, countries needed not only non-proliferation controls but also secure materials, safe operations, capable regulators, trained personnel and strong national institutions. AI can transform healthcare, education, agriculture, energy, manufacturing, public administration and research, helping developing countries overcome barriers. Yet it also brings job displacement, misinformation, cyberattacks, fraud and potentially harmful autonomous decision-making. The question is how to keep this power aligned with progress without letting its destructive potential escape control. While the IAEA experience is relevant, WAICO should not copy the Agency. AI is software-based, diffuse, fast-moving and developed by thousands of private actors. Nevertheless, the IAEA’s institutional logic offers five useful lessons. Risk management cannot be separated from development: Governance cannot be framed only as restriction. For many developing countries, the priority is access. A regime in which advanced states possess AI while others merely follow rules designed elsewhere will deepen inequality. So, WAICO should make capacity building a central pillar. China’s plan to offer developing countries 5,000 AI training and seminar opportunities over five years and establish international application centres could become a permanent multilateral programme. It should build national capacity — universities, research institutions, regulators, data infrastructure, etc. — much as IAEA technical cooperation has done in the nuclear field. Develop an AI safeguards concept: Trust cannot rest on declarations. AI safeguards should not block access but identify exceptionally powerful capabilities, manage their risks and verify commitments. A risk-based system could grade capabilities, set standards, require transparency, establish testing methods, and independently assess declared advanced systems through continuous monitoring and peer review like the IAEA verification and peer review system. It should focus on consequential applications, not intrusively control every system. AI safety should be an international public good: This is necessary because failures and malicious use can cross borders. WAICO could develop shared principles, standards, testing methods and incident-reporting mechanisms, and enable countries to share failures and near misses so others can prevent their recurrence. IAEA safety standards and operating experience systems show how consensus guidance and corrective learning can reduce risk without assigning blame. Security must be distinguished from safety: Safety addresses accidents, failures and unintended harm; security addresses deliberate misuse, manipulation and attack. Distinguishing between them would support clearer legal, regulatory and ethical responses. Standards aren’t enough — people and institutions matter: Standards work only when countries have capable institutions and people. WAICO could create regional centres of excellence along with training, fellowships, laboratories and regulatory capacity programmes, helping developing countries implement commitments similar to IAEA technical cooperation programmes. WAICO should learn from the IAEA but not become the IAEA of AI. AI differs fundamentally from nuclear technology. Nuclear material can be physically controlled and is concentrated in capital-intensive facilities; AI software can be copied, modified and distributed instantly. WAICO cannot transplant the IAEA model, but it can adopt its balanced approach: enable beneficial use, build capacity, set safety and security standards, and prevent misuse. The international community has spent nearly 70 years learning to govern a beneficial but dangerous technology. The IAEA also has its limitations and is politically constrained, yet WAICO should study its successes, failures and adaptations rather than reinvent the wheel. Eisenhower sought to turn the atom from an instrument of destruction into a force for peace. Today, the challenge is to ensure that AI serves humanity rather than subordinates or harms it. WAICO should place safety and security alongside development and capacity building; promote cooperation without blocking developing country access; set international standards that respect national contexts; and focus oversight on the gravest risks rather than every application. In 1953, the world answered Eisenhower’s call and created the IAEA. Today, Xi has called for AI to become “an important driver for shared prosperity and common security”. The world should respond with equal seriousness. Shahid Ahmed Mallick was director at IAEA and Aftab Ahmad Khokher was ambassador in Austria/IAEA.
articles.author: Shahid Ahmed Mallick | Aftab Ahmad Khokher

articles.title: ‘Tales of ancients’
articles.content: NIGHT falls upon Ibrahim and he sees a star. “This is my Lord,” he says. But when it sets, he declares that he does not love things that disappear. The moon rises, larger and more luminous, but it too passes. Then the sun appears in overwhelming splendour. “This is greater,” he says — until the sun also sets. Ibrahim finally turns beyond all created brilliance towards the One who brought the heavens and the earth into being (6:76-79). This is a powerful parable of the quest for God. Ibrahim does not begin with a formula. He looks, wonders, tests and moves beyond each inadequate answer. The star, moon and sun carry real beauty and power. Yet none can be Rabb — the sustaining Lord — because each is contingent, governed and destined to disappear. The seeker must pass through the visible sign to the invisible Source, from the splendour of creation to its Creator. If read only as ancient religious history, the passage records the rejection by Ibrahim of celestial worship. Read as guidance, it describes an inward journey that must be undertaken repeatedly. What brilliant but temporary thing have I mistaken for the centre of my life? Wealth, status, tribe, ideology, technology and even inherited religious authority can become stars and suns of the self when they demand allegiance belonging to God alone. The scholar Laleh Bakhtiar invites the reader to discover “the Abraham of one’s being”. The phrase turns admiration into responsibility. Ibrahim represents the faculty within us that can question inherited falsehood, withstand social pressure and turn towards what is enduring. But if there is an Ibrahim within us, there is also an idol-maker: that part of the self which prefers the approval of the crowd and fashions absolutes out of its desires. The Quran repeats moments of moral consequence. The Quran tells us that its stories carry guidance for those who understand: “In their stories there is truly a lesson for people of reason. …” (12:111). Yet familiarity can blunt their force. We hear of Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Yusuf and Yunus so often that they may become figures in a sacred history — revered, but removed from the disorder of our lives. The Quran does not offer prophetic biography in the modern sense, nor does it address our curiosity about dates and places. It selects and repeats moments of moral consequence. Its purpose is not merely to tell us what once happened but to reveal what continues to happen within human beings and societies. To confine these narratives to the past is to reduce them to the very charge the Quran reports: “asatirul awwalin”, “tales of the ancients”. The prophets disclose different aspects of moral life. Adam shows the human tendency to become conscious of shame and seek words of repentance. Nuh embodies perseverance when truth appears to produce no immediate result. Musa approaches pharaoh despite confessing fear; courage in the Quran is not the absence of fear but obedience despite it. Yusuf refuses both seduction and revenge. When power passes into his hands, he does not reproduce the cruelty once inflicted upon him. Yunus, by contrast, walks away in anger and discovers that commitment to a righteous cause does not place a person beyond correction. Prophethood carries divine authority, but the Quran permits us to see moments of vulnerability and anguish. Nuh grieves for his son. Yaqub’s eyes whiten with sorrow. Musa strikes a man and immediately recognises the gravity of his act. Muhammad (PBUH) is consoled and strengthened. Their exemplary character becomes accessible because revelation shows moral greatness being exercised under pressure. To call the prophets role models, therefore, is correct but insufficient. A role model may remain outside us, an object of admiration. The Quranic prophet is also a mirror, a warner and a summoner. Each narrative asks: where is pharaoh operating now — in the state, the institution, the family, or the commanding self? What prison has preserved our integrity? Whom must we forgive when we possess the power to retaliate? From what necessary task are we trying to flee? This mode of reading prevents religion from becoming sentimental. Love for the prophets cannot be confined to praise, recitation or commemoration. To honour Ibrahim while protecting our idols, to celebrate Musa while accommodating tyranny, or to admire Yusuf while nursing revenge is to keep the story at a safe distance from its demand. The Quran gives us recurring patterns rather than relics of a vanished world. Its prophetic narratives travel across time because arrogance, fear, envy, patience, repentance and courage travel with humans. The decisive question is not whether these stories are true only of the past. It is whether, through them, we are prepared to recognise the truth about ourselves. The writer is lecturer, Aga Khan University Faculty of Arts and Science.
articles.author: Abbas Hussain

articles.title: Container city
articles.content: EVEN after butchering local ecologies and evicting tens of thousands from their decades-old homes, they insist on calling it Islamabad the beautiful. It really ought to be called Container City. The federal capital — and its twin city, Rawalpindi — once again resembles a loading dock for cargo ships. And as always, we are told that besieging the twin cities is in the greater national interest. The fact that official definitions of the national interest are completely unrelated to popular sentiment is not a new quandary for the powers that be. But in comparison to almost every other dispensation in Pakistan’s history, this regime is not bothered with gaining even a modicum of consent from the people, having liberally deployed the big stick in the country’s core regions to match what has always been the historical norm in the peripheries. Barely veiled threats have been issued this time too, ‘violent groups’ warned against trying to enter Islamabad. There have been a series of pre-emptive strikes against anyone and everyone that the government designates a ‘security risk’. From Imran Khan’s elderly sisters to the president of the Islamabad street vendors’ association, the regime is intent on ensuring that it alienates even those who have no link to the PTI. Whether the latter’s ‘long march’ even materialises is irrelevant, because the optics of a heavily contained population is the real story. The container city, in fact, is a microcosm of the country at large. If you have a dissenting political opinion, you can be locked up, issued a Peca notice, or maybe even disappeared. To aspire to an economic situation beyond bare survival requires one to work longer and harder for slave wages — if you are amongst those from the army of unemployed that can actually find work. The container city is a microcosm of the country at large. It should not go unnoticed that Islamabad’s police officials have asked for Rs827 million to manage the yet-to-happen protests. Meanwhile, there is no suggestion that even a pittance of that sum will be allocated to upgrade facilities and quality of services in PIMS in the wake of thehorrific firewhich claimed the lives of 14 newborns. There is no pretence at play here, no meaningful hegemonic strategy. The only consistent and conscious interest of the regime is in the realm of geopolitics. But unlike authoritarian rule under Ayub, Zia and Musharraf, today’s rulers cannot count on a structural windfall due to favourable geopolitical winds. Aside from acquiring geostrategic rents from anti-communist Seato and Cento pacts, the Ayub regime actually had an industrial policy, cultivating something resembling a manufacturing sector and absorbing some labouring masses displaced from the agrarian sector. The 22 families, including emergent state profiteers, may have captured the major spoils, but there was some logic to the regime’s claim that a little wealth would eventually ‘trickle down’ to the masses. Even while presiding over de-industrialisation, Zia benefited from the Gulf remittances as well as big industrial investments made under the Bhutto dispensation, not to mention windfalls from the ‘Afghan jihad’. Musharraf came to power after industrial policy was definitively declared dead, but the dictatorship nevertheless benefited from post 9/11 remittances and ‘war on terror’ dollars. The current dispensation only secures fuel to keep government running the next day by extorting the masses through a levy, while its economic imagination is limited to FDI and a developmental logic revolving around resource grabs. It has shut down border trade with Afghanistan, which is a major supply of the everyday economy. Meanwhile, members of the Pakistani bourgeoisie itself lament its comprador character, the CEO of the Sentinel Group recently penning a telling essay on ‘Pakistan’s missing multinationals’. To be sure, the rot extends much deeper than the present regime. The so-called ‘demographic dividend’ which has been hyped up for at least 15 years is, instead, a huge pressure cooker; neither the state nor the private bourgeoisie — and for the most part this nexus operates in unison — has the capacity or interest to develop the skills of an exceedingly young population let alone guarantee it a dignified income. And where young and old working people alike demonstrate enterprise so as to make ends meet, the response of the state is to suppress, confiscate, even destroy. Look no further than the treatment of Islamabad’s katchi abadi dwellers and street vendors in recent months. Containment of the political and economic freedoms of Pakistan’s teeming masses is what the militarised state apparatus knows best. But building container cities does not make acute contradictions disappear, they only magnify them. The writer teaches at Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad.
articles.author: Aasim Sajjad Akhtar

articles.title: Palestine in focus
articles.content: ISRAEL’S barbaric violence in Gaza, as well as rampages by extremist Jewish settlers in the West Bank, have earned the Zionist state the opprobrium of several states during the ongoing UN General Assembly. While the impassioned speeches will not be enough to stop the violence against the Palestinian people, they do indicate that even some of Israel’s allies in the West are having a difficult time justifying its monstrous behaviour. French President Emmanuel Macron said the “spectacle” in Gaza should “shame us all”. He also highlighted the grim situation in the West Bank. Similarly, Turkish President Recep Erdogan termed Gaza an “inhumane … concentration camp”. At a separate meeting on the two-state solution, Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Darslammedthe Israeli “machinery of occupation”. At the same event, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said “time is running out” for the two-state solution. Perhaps the outgoing UN head was being overly optimistic — Israel has done all possible to ensure a viable Palestinian state does not emerge. Not too far from these meetings the Board of Peace was also holding a session,pledging$2.45bn for Gaza’s ‘recovery’. While the promise of these funds should be welcomed, the reality in the occupied Strip tempers any hopes for Gaza’s betterment. After all, since last year’sceasefireIsrael has murdered some 1,400 people in Gaza, mostly civilians, while Tel Aviv has refused to end its occupation of the Strip, even though Hamas agreed to give up its arms. Meanwhile, illegal settlements have exploded in the West Bank, with Jewish settlers growing more vicious in their attacks by the day. Therefore, throwing money at Gaza will do little if the Palestinians remain under siege, and the theft of their land continues. If conscientious members of the international community are serious about their concern for Palestine, they must back their talk with action. Israel must be held to account for its genocidal violence in Gaza, while settlers in the West Bank should be punished for their occupation of Palestinian land, and frequent physical attacks on Arabs. All illegal settlements need to be uprooted. Sadly, while calls for a two-state solution continue, the current Israeli regime — and whatever dispensation emerges after the coming elections in the Zionist state — will remain hell-bent on preventing a sovereign Palestinian state from emerging. Meanwhile, Israel’s most powerful foreign patron — the US — seems utterly uninterested in making Tel Aviv commit itself to the peace process. PR stunts under the Board of Peace are one thing; genuine pressure on Israel to end the occupation is another. Can the Palestinian people expect relief when such powerful actors remain committed to prolonging their suffering?
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: The IMF loop
articles.content: IF anything, the IMF reviews capture the paradox of Pakistan’s economic management. The numbers may be improving, but the economy itself remains largely unchanged. The government is meeting some fiscal and monetary targets while missing reforms that would alter how the state and markets actually function. There is something increasingly tiring about watching these IMF reviews. The IMF mission arrives. The government presents its case. Officials hold meetings. Statements are issued. Then the Fund’s assessment comes out, identifying almost exactly the same strengths and weaknesses that were previously pointed out. The purpose of the reviews cannot simply be to pass successive tests. Yet much of the economic effort still appears organised around precisely that objective: meet the quantitative targets, secure the next tranche and move on to the next review. The government has achieved an important degree of macroeconomic stability. Fiscal discipline has improved. Foreign exchange reserves have been rebuilt — even if they remain fragile. The external account is less precarious than it was. These are not small gains. But stability is supposed to create the space for reform and sustainable growth. It cannot become an end in itself. The more uncomfortable question is what has actually changed underneath the stabilisation numbers. The IMF itself continues to point to delayed critical reforms, market interventions, weak governance and missed social-sector spending. The government has also yet to fully implement several legislative and institutional changes agreed under the programme. This suggests a bigger problem. The government, like its predecessors, may be trying to complete the programme without fundamentally changing the economic model that repeatedly produces the need for such programmes. Once the programme is completed and reserves rebuilt, it may loosen the fiscal and monetary brakes to accelerate growth before the election. The temptation will be to spend the gains of stabilisation on a short-term growth push and flaunt the resulting numbers as economic success. We have been there before — not once, not twice, but more than two dozen times. The danger is repeating this cycle after the current programme. Growth must come from structural reform, not spending the gains of stability and returning to the IMF yet again.
articles.author: Editorial
